speaker: Rohan
text: Is the coffee machine on four still broken or is it just me?

speaker: Keiko
text: Still broken. Facilities said Thursday, maybe. I've been going down to the lobby place.

speaker: Aisha
text: You're a hero. OK, let's start. This is the offline mode review for the field technician app. Right now if a tech loses signal in a basement the app basically freezes, and support gets tickets every single day about checklists that vanished.

speaker: Rohan
text: Yeah. From the product side the bar is: a technician can work a whole shift with zero connectivity, so call it eight hours. They see their assigned jobs, fill in checklists, take photos, capture the customer's signature. And nothing they complete ever gets lost. That last one is the hard requirement.

speaker: Aisha
text: And just so we're clear on scope, two techs editing the same job at the same time, live, Google Docs style, we are not building that.

speaker: Rohan
text: Right, no live co-editing. A job is assigned to one tech, occasionally it gets reassigned, that's it.

speaker: Keiko
text: Some sizing so we're not guessing. About four thousand active technicians, roughly twelve jobs each per day. Photos are the heavy part, it's around twenty photos a job at maybe three megs each.

speaker: Daniel
text: On the device I'd just keep everything in SQLite. We already use it for the parts catalog cache, so the plumbing is there. Keiko, any objection?

speaker: Keiko
text: Yeah, SQLite on the device is fine by me.

speaker: Daniel
text: The bigger question is conflicts. I've been reading about CRDTs, and Automerge has a React Native binding now. If every job is a CRDT document we basically never have to think about merge logic again.

speaker: Keiko
text: I mean, it's elegant. But what's actually concurrent here? A dispatcher moves the appointment window, the tech fills in the checklist. Those are different fields. Nobody is typing into the same notes field at the same time.

speaker: Aisha
text: And the document history just grows, right? A phone that's been offline all day with twenty photos queued, I don't love it also carrying an ever-growing change log per job.

speaker: Keiko
text: Plus nobody on the backend team has run Automerge in production. We'd spend the quarter debugging the merge library instead of shipping.

speaker: Aisha
text: OK, I think CRDTs are out for this one. Too heavy for what is basically single-writer data, and nobody here has operated it. Keiko, what's the simpler version?

speaker: Keiko
text: Field-level last-writer-wins. Every field carries a version number that the server assigns. The client sends the version it last saw, and if the server has a newer one for that field, the server's value wins and we send it back down.

speaker: Daniel
text: Field-level, not row-level, so the dispatcher changing the time window doesn't stomp on the tech's checklist answers. OK, I can live with that.

speaker: Aisha
text: Good. So that's the conflict model: field-level last-writer-wins with server-assigned versions, for all work order fields.

speaker: Rohan
text: Small one. How long do completed jobs stay on the phone? Techs sometimes need to look up what they did last week.

speaker: Daniel
text: I was going to say seven days and then we purge them.

speaker: Rohan
text: Seven days works for me.

speaker: Keiko
text: Transport. My proposal is a small sync gateway, a WebSocket service. The app keeps a socket open while it's online, pushes its change batches up, and we push dispatcher changes down in real time.

speaker: Aisha
text: Real-time push down to the device would be really nice for reassignments. Daniel?

speaker: Daniel
text: There's a decent socket library for React Native. Sure, should be fine.

speaker: Aisha
text: OK, let's do the sync gateway then. It sits in front of the work order service.

speaker: Daniel
text: And for photos, the simplest thing is to send them inside the same change batch, as multipart, so a job and its photos always arrive together.

speaker: Keiko
text: Arriving together is nice for the back office, they hate seeing a completed job with no photos. Fine by me.

speaker: Aisha
text: Agreed, photos ride along in the change batch.

speaker: Rohan
text: Random idea: what if techs pre-download tomorrow's jobs over the depot Wi-Fi overnight, so they start the day fully loaded?

speaker: Keiko
text: Oh, sorry, going back to conflicts. There's one field that breaks last-writer-wins, which is status. If dispatch cancels a job while the tech is offline, and the tech then completes it, last-writer-wins just flips it to completed, or back to cancelled, depending on who synced last. Either way somebody's work silently disappears.

speaker: Aisha
text: Yeah, that's not really a last-writer-wins thing, that's a business rule. OK, let's narrow it. Last-writer-wins covers the fields the tech edits: notes, checklist answers, parts used, the signature. Status is taken out of that, and how we resolve a cancelled-versus-completed conflict is an open question.

speaker: Rohan
text: I'd want the ops managers in on that one. Sometimes they still bill the visit even if it was cancelled.

speaker: Daniel
text: Coming back to the socket for a sec. Let me dig into how iOS treats background sockets, I have a bad feeling about it.

speaker: Keiko
text: While you do that, batch sizing. I'd cap a sync request at two hundred changes. Honestly it's a guess, it just keeps the non-photo part of a request small.

speaker: Aisha
text: Then two hundred for the pilot, and we look at it again once we have real traffic.

speaker: Rohan
text: Can I ask about encryption? If a phone gets stolen, that local database has customer addresses and gate codes in it.

speaker: Daniel
text: We could use SQLCipher. It's basically a drop-in for SQLite, but there's a real cost. On the older Android devices our techs carry, opening the database gets noticeably slower, and the key has to live in the keystore.

speaker: Keiko
text: Or we rely on device encryption plus MDM. The phones are all company-managed, they're encrypted at rest anyway.

speaker: Daniel
text: I really don't want to take a thirty percent hit on app startup for something MDM already covers.

speaker: Keiko
text: Gate codes in plaintext on a lost phone isn't a great look either, though.

speaker: Aisha
text: I don't think we can settle this in this room. Rohan, can you take it to the security team and come back with their position?

speaker: Rohan
text: Yeah, I'll set that up.

speaker: Daniel
text: OK, so I looked at the background socket thing while you were talking about encryption. It's as bad as I thought. iOS kills the socket a few seconds after the app goes to the background, and Android's battery optimisation does much the same. So the socket is only alive while the tech is actually looking at the app.

speaker: Keiko
text: Which means the gateway buys us almost nothing. We'd need a fallback for the background case anyway.

speaker: Daniel
text: What I'd do instead: plain HTTPS delta sync on the existing work order API. The app pulls changes since its last cursor, and when dispatch changes something we send a silent push through APNs and FCM to wake the app up and trigger a pull.

speaker: Keiko
text: That's one less service for me to run, honestly. And the API already has auth and rate limiting.

speaker: Aisha
text: OK. We drop the sync gateway. Sync becomes an HTTPS delta endpoint on the work order API, triggered by silent push.

speaker: Keiko
text: Now that the batch goes through the normal API, I'm worried about putting photos in the batch. Twenty photos at three megs is sixty megs per job. If that upload dies at ninety percent on a flaky connection, the whole batch fails, checklist answers included.

speaker: Keiko
text: I'd reverse that one. Photos upload separately, straight to S3 with presigned URLs, resumable, on their own background queue. The change batch only carries the photo keys.

speaker: Aisha
text: Agreed, let's reverse it. The back office can live with a job showing photos still uploading for a while. Checklist data must never wait behind photos.

speaker: Rohan
text: Going back to how long jobs stay on the device. I talked to two of the regional leads last week. Warranty callbacks usually happen within two weeks, and techs want to see what they did on the first visit.

speaker: Daniel
text: So fourteen days instead? Storage-wise that's fine as long as photos get purged once they're uploaded. We'd only be keeping the job data.

speaker: Aisha
text: Fourteen days it is. Completed jobs stay on the device for fourteen days, and photos are deleted locally once the upload is confirmed.

speaker: Rohan
text: What about telling the tech when one of their edits lost a conflict?

speaker: Keiko
text: For the pilot I'd just log conflicts on the server. We don't even know how often they happen yet.

speaker: Aisha
text: Fine for now. Server-side logging only, and after the pilot we come back to whether techs need to see something.

speaker: Aisha
text: Let's do owners. Keiko, the sync API contract?

speaker: Keiko
text: I'll have the delta sync API contract written up by next Wednesday.

speaker: Daniel
text: And I want to check what Apple's throttling does to silent pushes. I've heard they get dropped if you send too many. I'll look into it.

speaker: Rohan
text: I'll grab time with the ops managers about the cancelled-versus-completed case too.

speaker: Aisha
text: Great. Anything else? No? OK, thanks everyone.
